before.quote:
A bounded wall domain is a bounded connected open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ with $C^2$ boundary. Its classical velocity class on $[0,T]$ is $C^1([0,T];C^2(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$; a pressure in this class is continuous in time with one continuous spatial derivative. The boundary normal $n$ is the outward unit normal. A no-slip trace is $u|_{\partial\Omega}=0$, a prescribed moving-wall trace is $u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$, and an impermeable trace is $u\cdot n=0$; these are distinct boundary data.

An exterior domain is $\Omega_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R^3\setminus K$, where $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ is compact with $C^2$ boundary and $\Omega_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is connected. The exterior classical velocity and pressure classes have the same local regularity up to $\partial K$ on every compact spatial subset. The domain definition alone imposes no condition at infinity. An exterior energy argument must state additional decay or weighted-space hypotheses. We call the explicit bounds $|u(t,x)|=O(|x|^{-2})$, $|\nabla u(t,x)|=O(|x|^{-3})$, and $|p(t,x)|=O(|x|^{-2})$, uniform for $t\in[0,T]$, a cutoff-decay condition; this is additional solution data, not part of the bare exterior domain, and no energy identity follows from this definition alone.

after.quote:
A bounded wall domain is a bounded connected open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ with $C^2$ boundary. For $T>0$, its classical velocity fields are maps $u:[0,T]\times\overline\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ in $C^1([0,T];C^2(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$, and its classical pressures are maps $p:[0,T]\times\overline\Omega\to\mathbb R$ in $C([0,T];C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R))$. Here spatial derivatives through the indicated order extend continuously to the boundary, and time continuity and differentiability are taken in the corresponding spatial supremum norms. The boundary normal $n$ is the outward unit normal. A no-slip trace is $u|_{\partial\Omega}=0$, a prescribed moving-wall trace is $u|_{\partial\Omega}=g$, and an impermeable trace is $u\cdot n=0$; these are distinct boundary data.

An exterior domain is $\Omega_{\mathrm{ext}}=\mathbb R^3\setminus K$, where $K\subset\mathbb R^3$ is compact with $C^2$ boundary and $\Omega_{\mathrm{ext}}$ is connected. The exterior classical fields are maps $u:[0,T]\times\overline\Omega_{\mathrm{ext}}\to\mathbb R^3$ and $p:[0,T]\times\overline\Omega_{\mathrm{ext}}\to\mathbb R$, with $u\in C^1([0,T];C^2_{\mathrm{loc}}(\overline\Omega_{\mathrm{ext}};\mathbb R^3))$ and $p\in C([0,T];C^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\overline\Omega_{\mathrm{ext}};\mathbb R))$. The local spaces require the indicated spatial derivatives to extend continuously up to $\partial K$; their topology is uniform convergence of those derivatives on each compact subset of the closure. The domain definition alone imposes no condition at infinity. An exterior energy argument must state additional decay or weighted-space hypotheses. We call the explicit bounds $|u(t,x)|=O(|x|^{-2})$, $|\nabla u(t,x)|=O(|x|^{-3})$, and $|p(t,x)|=O(|x|^{-2})$, uniform for $t\in[0,T]$, a cutoff-decay condition; this is additional solution data, not part of the bare exterior domain, and no energy identity follows from this definition alone.

before.quote:
Let $d\ge2$ be an integer, and let $L>0$ be the numerical period in a fixed
length unit. Let
$\mathbb T_L^d=(\mathbb R/L\mathbb Z)^d$ carry normalized Lebesgue measure
$L^{-d}dx$. For $k\in\mathbb Z^d$ put
$\kappa_k=2\pi k/L$ and $e_k(x)=\exp(i\kappa_k\cdot x)$. For a complex
scalar or vector $L^2$ class $f$, let
$\widehat f(k)=L^{-d}\int_{[0,L]^d}f(x)e^{-i\kappa_k\cdot x}\,dx$;
real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$. For $s\ge0$, let
$$H^s(\mathbb T_L^d)=\left\{f\in L^2:\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^s|\widehat f(k)|^2<\infty\right\},$$
with norm given by the square root of this sum; the weight is dimensionless.
Under Countable Choice the coefficient map is injective, so this is a norm.
The real solenoidal spaces are
$$H=\{u\in L^2(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d): k\cdot\widehat u(k)=0\text{ for every }k\ne0\},\qquad V=H\cap H^1(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb R^d).$$
The zero Fourier mode is unrestricted. Under Countable Choice, the supplied
Fourier-basis theorem makes the coefficient map a surjective isometry from
$L^2$ onto $\ell^2$; the coefficient-space norm identifications and the
equivalence between Fourier divergence and distributional divergence in this
definition use that hypothesis. Under the same assumption, the orthogonal
solenoidal projection $P$ is well-defined on $L^2$ and has multiplier
$P_0=I$ and
$P_k=I-\kappa_k\kappa_k^{\mathsf T}/|\kappa_k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. For integer
$N\ge0$, rectangular truncation $\Pi_N$ keeps precisely $|k|_\infty\le N$. A weak
derivative in coordinate $j$ has Fourier coefficient $i\kappa_{k,j}\widehat f(k)$.
For $r>0$, $H^{-r}$ is the Hilbert completion of finite complex Fourier
coefficient sequences in the norm squared
$\sum_k(1+L^2|\kappa_k|^2)^{-r}|\widehat f(k)|^2$; its real subspace is the
completion of the conjugate-symmetric sequences.

real fields are the classes satisfying
$\widehat f(-k)=\overline{\widehat f(k)}$.

The periodic scalar test functions are $C^\infty(\mathbb T_L^d;\mathbb C)$, identified with smooth $L$-periodic lifts to $\mathbb R^d$ and equipped with the seminorms
$$p_m(\varphi)=\max_{|\alpha|\le m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb T_L^d}|\partial^\alpha\varphi(x)|\qquad(m\in\mathbb N_0).$$

$L^2$ onto $\ell^2$; the coefficient-space norm identifications and the
equivalence between Fourier divergence and distributional divergence in this
definition use that hypothesis. Under the same assumption, the orthogonal
solenoidal projection $P$ is well-defined on $L^2$ and has multiplier
$P_0=I$ and
$P_k=I-\kappa_k\kappa_k^{\mathsf T}/|\kappa_k|^2$ for $k\ne0$. For integer
$N\ge0$, rectangular truncation $\Pi_N$ keeps precisely $|k|_\infty\le N$. A weak

before.quote:
For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\to\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions.

after.quote:
Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. For the fixed-support spaces of [[def-fixed-support-test-function-frechet-space]], let $\mathcal P$ be the set of all seminorms $q:\mathcal D(\Omega)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $q|_{\mathcal D_K}$ is continuous for every compact $K\subseteq\Omega$. A seminorm means $q(av)=|a|q(v)$ and $q(v+w)\le q(v)+q(w)$.

The **test-function topology** is the topology generated by translated finite intersections of sets $\{\varphi:q(\varphi)<\varepsilon\}$, where $q\in\mathcal P$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Equivalently it is the finest locally convex topology making every inclusion $\mathcal D_K\hookrightarrow\mathcal D(\Omega)$ continuous; the universal-property lemma below proves this equivalence and the topology assertions. This is the locally convex inductive-limit or **LF topology**, not the unrestricted final topology of arbitrary spaces.

For precision, a locally convex topology here is a vector topology generated by a family of seminorms, and boundedness means absorption by every zero-neighborhood: for each such neighborhood $U$ there is $t>0$ with $B\subseteq tU$. Finite intersections may be empty, giving the whole space. When $\Omega$ is empty there is only the zero vector and its unique topology. No convergence criterion for sequences is used in the definition; that criterion will be a theorem.
